We can now explicitly describe the sections of unramified morphisms.

<STRUCT_0001>
<LOCKED_0001>
Let <MATH_0001> be a connected scheme.
Let <MATH_0002> be unramified and separated.
Every section of <MATH_0003> is an isomorphism onto a connected component.
There exists a bijective correspondence
<MATHSEG_0001>sections of <MATHSEG_0002>connected components <MATHSEG_0003> of <MATHSEG_0004> such that<MATHSEG_0005>the induced map <MATHSEG_0006> is an isomorphism<MATHSEG_0007>
In particular, given <MATH_0004> there is at most one
section passing through <MATH_0005>.

<STRUCT_0001>
The preceding theorem gives us some idea of the ``rigidity'' of unramified
morphisms. Further indication is provided by the following proposition
which, besides being intrinsically interesting, is also useful in the
theory of the algebraic fundamental group (see <REF_0001>).
See also the more general
Morphisms, Lemma <REF_0002>.

<STRUCT_0001>
<LOCKED_0001>
Sections of unramified morphisms.
<STRUCT_0002>
<STRUCT_0003> Any section of an unramified morphism is an open immersion.
<STRUCT_0004> Any section of a separated morphism is a closed immersion.
<STRUCT_0005> Any section of an unramified separated morphism is open and closed.
<STRUCT_0006>
<STRUCT_0007>
